summary: The note gives an overview of space weather, meaning solar flares, coronal mass ejections and solar wind, and how solar storms affect satellites, GPS, power grids, communication networks and aviation. It cites several dated incidents in autumn 2023 and quotes experts on the risks. It closes with the protective measures under way and the need for monitoring and collaboration as the sun's 11-year cycle heads toward its peak.
one_line: Overview of space weather and solar storms, their 2023 impacts on satellites, GPS, power grids, networks and aviation, and mitigation efforts.
key_facts: Space weather comprises conditions originating from the sun, including solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and solar wind.
On October 14, 2023, astronomers at NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory spotted an active sunspot region hurling a significant solar flare towards Earth.
Dr. Emily Peterson, a solar physicist, said the sun undergoes an 11-year cycle and is currently ramping up towards the peak, increasing the frequency of solar storms.
Charged particles from flares and CMEs travel the 93-millionmile distance between the sun and Earth and can induce geomagnetic storms when they hit Earth's magnetosphere.
On September 22, 2023, a geomagnetic storm sparked by a previous CME caused auroral displays seen as far south as Colorado.
Thomas Riley of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation said currents induced by geomagnetic storms can exceed the tolerances of power infrastructure.

On September 15, 2023, a geostationary satellite temporarily lost its orientation due to a mild solar storm, interrupting weather forecasting and telecommunications for several hours, according to mission director Johnathan Hughes.
On October 3, 2023, airline pilot Maria Gonzales had to switch to backup navigation systems until the GPS signal stabilized because of ionospheric fluctuations.
A powerful geomagnetic storm akin to the Carrington Event of 1859 could have catastrophic consequences for modern electricity-dependent infrastructure.
On October 20, 2023, utility companies across North America conducted a coordinated drill to test their resilience to space weather events.
Protective measures for electricity infrastructure include geomagnetically induced current (GIC) monitoring systems, more robust transformers, and adaptive grid configurations.

On September 29, 2023, a minor solar flare disrupted satellite links for transoceanic communications, temporarily slowing internet traffic; network strategist Linda Webb said routing protocols that adapt quickly are being developed.
Fiber-optic cables are largely immune to space weather's direct effects, but the electronic components managing data transmission are not.
After a November 2, 2023 incident in which communication with several transatlantic flights was degraded by a solar storm, aviation authorities stressed continuous monitoring and training.
